title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
hookLine: after the great catch Peter falls down: I am a sinful man

cards: Fishermen on the lake of Genesareth worked at night, when the fish came up toward the surface. So picture the morning. Simon and his partners have been out all night and caught nothing.
They're on the shore, washing their nets, tired and done. A crowd presses in on a teacher, who climbs into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little, so he can talk to the people from the water.
When he's finished, he says what no tired fisherman wants to hear: go back out. Let down your nets again. In the daytime.

teach.h: AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.
teach.b: Simon's answer is honest and a little weary: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net."

teach.h: THE NETS BREAK, THE BOATS SINK.
teach.b: And the nets fill so full they begin to break. He waves for the other boat, James and John, and both boats load up until they start to sink. You'd expect a fisherman to celebrate.
Instead Luke says Simon Peter fell down at Jesus' knees: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." It's strange. Nobody accused Peter of anything.
But being that close to something holy made him see himself clearly, and what he saw made him want distance. Isaiah felt it in the Temple, crying out that he was a man of unclean lips.
Jesus doesn't argue with Peter about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't leave, either. He says: "Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men."
Peter asks for distance and gets a job. Then a quiet line: they brought their boats to land, and leaving all things, they followed him. Catholics hear an echo of this at every Mass.
Just before Communion, the people say they are not worthy to receive the Lord, and ask him only to say the word.

teach.h: DEPART FROM ME, FOR I AM A SINFUL MAN.
teach.b: Those words come from a Roman centurion a little later in Luke, but the instinct is Peter's on the beach: I'm not ready for you to come this close. And in both stories, he comes anyway.

how: Catholics hear Luke's call of Peter at Sunday Mass in the year Luke's Gospel is read, and before Communion the whole congregation says aloud that they are not worthy, asking the Lord only to say the word.

o: the town where Peter grew up fishing
the lake where Peter made his great catch
the river where John baptized Jesus

games.q: the great catch — tap the pairs.

so full they began to break
depart from me, I am a sinful man

s: Peter celebrated the catch as the best day of his career
he fell at Jesus' knees and asked him to depart, because he felt like a sinful man.
Jesus told Peter he wasn't really a sinner
he didn't argue the point. he said fear not, and gave him a new job.
the words before Communion at Mass come from a centurion in Luke
Luke 7:6–7: he says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof.

games.q: you're Simon. you fished all night and caught nothing. a teacher tells you to go back out in daylight. what do you do?
o: explain politely that it's the wrong time of day.
say we caught nothing, but at your word I'll let down the net.
games.why: he says both things at once: the honest complaint and the yes. the nets fill until they break.

practice: Notice one thing in you that makes you want to keep God, or anyone good, at arm's length: a habit, a regret, a mood you're in today.

Don't fix it; just name it, the way Peter named his, and then picture the answer he got: not a lecture, just fear not, and an invitation to stay in the boat. If you pray, say Peter's words, and rest in the silence after them.

wordCard.voice: Genesareth. The lake where Peter's great catch left him saying depart from me, until Jesus answered, fear not. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fear not, or stop being afraid. Jesus' answer to Peter in Luke 5:10.

carryVoice: Your line: fear not. The answer Jesus gave to I'm not ready. See you tomorrow.
